title: The Night the Lights Went Out
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
The generator failed with a sound like a very large person clearing their throat.

Then the entire eastern side of Lanternwell Square went dark.

I was at Brasswatch Yard with Danse, checking the volunteer repair schedule. One moment the workshop lights were humming; the next they were gone. Outside, somebody shouted. A few seconds later the emergency lantern by the door came on.

Danse was already moving.

"Stay back from the panel," he said.

"I wasn't planning to touch it."

"Good."

He opened the insulated access cover and looked at the gauges. The smell of overheated wiring hung in the air, sharp and unpleasant. The generator had been carrying extra load since the storm flooded the lower service route. We knew it needed inspection. We hadn't expected it to fail tonight.

A runner arrived from the square.

"The hall's dark. People are sheltering from the weather."

Danse looked at the panel.

"I can restore power."

"When?"

He hesitated.

"Not until I know what failed."

That was the right answer, though it hurt to hear it.

We brought the portable lanterns to the hall. Maui was already carrying blankets to the west benches. Katara was checking that the children had their caregivers nearby. Neri had a paper list of people who had chosen to wait there, with no public record of private destinations.

I helped set lanterns where they wouldn't block the exit.

Danse spoke to the volunteers.

"We need a trained person at the generator, two people to watch the backup lamps, and someone to check the cables for water damage. No one enters the electrical room without protective equipment."

He didn't assign people by pointing at them. He asked who was trained and available.

Renn raised a hand.

"I can check the cable run. I trained on that system last week."

Danse looked at them.

"With me."

Aster volunteered for the backup lamps. Pip offered to maintain the clear path, then asked to be relieved after an hour.

Everything moved more slowly than a military emergency would have.

It also moved with people who knew what they'd agreed to do.

We found the fault near the old canal service junction. Water had reached an improperly sealed conduit. One breaker had tripped, and the generator's load control had tried to compensate until it shut down.

Danse stared at the panel.

"I approved that conduit inspection last month."

"Was it completed?" I asked.

He checked the log.

"No."

I felt a cold knot in my stomach.

"Then we document that."

He nodded.

There would be time later for accountability. Right now we needed safe lights, dry equipment, and a plan that didn't make the next repair more dangerous than the outage itself.

Renn tested the replacement cable while Danse checked the voltage. Aster reported that two backup lamps were losing power. We moved the remaining lights to the highest-traffic routes and made sure people knew which corridors were still dark.

No one was ordered to stay in the hall.

No one was forced through a Threadway.

Near midnight, a deep note sounded from the direction of Tideglass. The second bell.

Danse looked toward the door.

"Pressure in the lower route," he said.

"Could it affect the generator?"

"Possibly. We should assume the service junction is still wet until we test it."

He refused to restart the system immediately.

A few people complained.

One man shouted that the old Brotherhood would have had the lights back already.

Danse looked at him.

"The old Brotherhood might have ordered someone into a flooded electrical room. That doesn't make it safe."

The man stopped.

I watched Danse turn back to the panel.

It was a small victory, but one he'd earned with work rather than a speech.

The backup power held until dawn. When the water level fell, the team completed the insulation test, replaced the damaged seal, and restarted the generator at reduced load. Lights returned to the workshop first, then the square.

There was no applause.

There was a list of repairs.

We posted the temporary load limit, the inspection results, and the next scheduled test. Renn added their signature beside the work they'd actually performed. Danse added his to the line documenting the missed conduit inspection.

By the time the last lantern was collected, my hands were shaking with exhaustion.

Danse noticed.

"You're cold."

"I'm tired."

"Then come home."

"There's still work."

"There's always work."

He said it with such quiet conviction that I looked up.

"Are you sure?"

"Renn and Aster have the next shift. Tamsin will review the repair. I've left the equipment in a safe state."

I nodded.

We walked to his room above the workshop. The familiar smell of clean metal and dry wood met me as he opened the door. He set the toolbelt aside, took off his coat, and stood for a moment looking at the lamp on the table.

"I used to feel better only when the lights came back," he said.

"And now?"

"Now I feel better knowing nobody was hurt because I wanted to restore them too quickly."

I took his hand.

"That matters."

He turned toward me.

"Do you want to stay?"

"Yes."

"Because you want to, not because it's late?"

I smiled.

"Both can be true."

He laughed softly.

His kiss was careful at first, then warmer when I rested my hands against his chest. We stood close enough to hear the rain easing outside. No one needed a heroic performance from us.

When he asked if I wanted to go inside, I said yes.

We closed the door and left the rest of the night private.

In the morning, there was a note from Renn.

The generator had passed its second test.

Underneath, in smaller writing, they had added: THANK YOU FOR NOT RUSHING.

Danse read it twice.

Then he folded it and put it in his pocket.
